library-a-tiny-seed-page-00-3: Nicola Rijsdijk & Maya Marshak Little Island Library adaptation.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-01-1: In a village on the slopes of Mount Kenya in East Africa, a little girl worked in the fields with her mother.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-02-2: In her family’s food garden she broke up the soil with her machete.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-02-3: She pressed tiny seeds into the warm earth.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-03-1: Her favourite time of day was just after sunset.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-03-2: When it got too dark to see the plants, Wangari knew it was time to go home.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-03-3: She would follow the narrow paths through the fields, crossing rivers as she went.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-04-review: Wangari’s big brother asked why she did not go to school with him. Her mother agreed to send her. Wangari later said she loved learning to read and write.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-05-2: Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-05-3: She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-05-5: She wanted to know more about the world.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-06-1: At the American university Wangari learnt many new things.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-06-2: She studied plants and how they grow.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-06-3: And she remembered how she grew: playing games with her brothers in the shade of the trees in the beautiful Kenyan forests.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-07-1: The more she learnt, the more she realised that she loved the people of Kenya.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-07-2: She wanted them to be happy and free.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-07-3: The more she learnt, the more she remembered her African home.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-08-review: After her studies, Wangari returned to Kenya. She listened to rural women who needed firewood, food and clean water. Trees and streams that their families relied on were being lost.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-09-review: Wangari worked with women to grow and plant trees. Their work became the Green Belt Movement. Together, they cared for the land and worked to improve life in their communities.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-10-review: The movement grew. Women and their communities planted millions of trees in Kenya. People in other African countries took up the idea too.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-11-2: People all over the world took notice, and gave her a famous prize.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-11-3: It is called the Nobel Peace Prize, and she was the first African woman ever to receive it.
library-a-tiny-seed-page-12-1: Wangari died in 2011, but we can think of her every time we see a beautiful tree.

library-airplanes-deep-4: Pressure differences and flow turning describe the same interaction in related ways.

library-blue-sky-deep-2: Much blue light has been scattered away, leaving more red and orange light.
library-blue-sky-deep-3: Never look straight at the Sun, even near sunset.

library-blue-sky-deep-5: Tiny air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths, including blue, more strongly than longer wavelengths such as red.

library-boats-float-deep-1: Archimedes’ principle relates the buoyant force to the weight of displaced fluid.
library-boats-float-deep-2: A floating boat settles until the upward force balances its weight, including its load.
library-boats-float-deep-3: Hull shape makes space that can remain largely filled with air, lowering the average density of the boat and its contents.
library-boats-float-deep-4: Adding load makes the hull sit lower and displace more water, up to its safe limits.
library-boats-float-deep-5: If water fills that space or the load is too great, floating can fail.
library-boats-float-deep-6: Stability matters too: an object can float but tip easily.
library-boats-float-deep-7: Our cross-section omits waves, leaks and balance changes; it is not boating or water-safety advice.

library-bones-deep-1: Bone combines a strong mineral-containing structure with living cells and a protein framework.
library-bones-deep-2: It is continually remodeled as some tissue is removed and new tissue is made.
library-bones-deep-3: Bones support the body, protect organs and provide attachment points for muscles.
library-bones-deep-4: Marrow inside certain bones makes blood cells.
library-bones-deep-5: Cartilage and other tissues help joints work; a skeleton alone cannot move itself.
library-bones-deep-6: People’s bodies and movement supports differ, and a picture of one skeleton is not a standard everyone must fit.
library-bones-deep-7: Food, activity suited to the person and healthcare all play roles in bone health.

library-breathing-deep-2: Their thin walls allow gas exchange: oxygen enters blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.
library-breathing-deep-3: The diaphragm is a muscle beneath the lungs.
library-breathing-deep-4: When it contracts and moves downward, space in the chest increases and air flows in.
library-breathing-deep-5: When it relaxes, air can flow out.
library-breathing-deep-6: The brain usually adjusts breathing without a conscious plan, responding to the body’s needs.
library-breathing-deep-7: Lungs do not create oxygen, and breathing is not a contest for the longest pause.

library-guam-more-3: An island is land with water all around it.
library-guam-more-4: A map helps show where Guam sits within a much larger ocean.
library-guam-more-5: Its reefs, forests, and hills are different parts of one connected island.
library-guam-rail-deep-1: Rails use dense vegetation for cover as they search near the ground for food.
library-guam-rail-deep-2: The Guam rail evolved on an island without the introduced brown treesnake.
library-guam-rail-deep-3: When snakes spread, many native birds faced predation they were poorly equipped to escape.
library-guam-rail-deep-4: Conservation breeding and carefully managed releases have been important parts of helping the rail.
library-guam-rail-deep-5: Habitat protection and control of introduced predators are also needed; simply opening a cage is not a recovery plan.
library-guam-rail-deep-6: Conservation status and release populations change, so this draft does not give a current population count or promise that a rail lives at a particular walking spot.
library-guam-rail-deep-7: The picture is an original simplified bird, not identification evidence.
library-guam-rail-more-1: The Guam rail is a small, mostly ground-living bird native to Guam.
library-guam-rail-more-2: Its wings are short and it is considered flightless.
library-guam-rail-more-3: Introduced brown treesnakes were a major cause of its loss from the wild on Guam.
library-guam-rail-more-4: Breeding and conservation work have helped keep the species from disappearing.
library-guam-rail-more-5: Watching wildlife kindly means giving it room.
library-guam-rail-tell-1: The Guam rail is a bird.
library-guam-rail-tell-3: People work to help this rare bird.
library-guam-tell-2: The Pacific Ocean is all around it.
library-guam-tell-3: It is part of the Mariana Islands.
library-habitats-deep-1: A habitat can be a coral reef, a wetland, a forest, or many other places.
library-habitats-deep-2: A nest is only one part of a bird's habitat.
library-habitats-deep-3: The whole surrounding area must meet its needs too.
library-habitats-deep-4: Habitat suitability depends on the needs of a particular species.
library-habitats-deep-5: A place that works for one animal may lack the food, water, shelter, or space another requires.
library-habitats-deep-6: These needs also depend on how the resources are arranged.
library-habitats-deep-7: A nest alone does not supply every need of a bird, just as a small patch of coral does not describe every place a reef animal uses.
library-habitats-deep-8: When we explain a habitat match, naming the resource is stronger evidence than saying the picture looks right.

library-hearing-deep-1: The three small middle-ear bones transfer vibrations toward the cochlea, a curled structure in the inner ear.
library-hearing-deep-2: Waves in its fluid move a membrane and the sensory hair cells on it.
library-hearing-deep-3: Bending tiny projections on these cells helps create electrical signals.
library-hearing-deep-4: Different places along the cochlea respond to different sound frequencies.
library-hearing-deep-5: The auditory nerve carries information to the brain; no little voice travels down a hollow nerve.
library-hearing-deep-6: Loud sounds can harm hearing, so the model needs no loud-noise test.
library-hearing-deep-7: Our spiral is an enlarged symbol of the cochlea, and the drawn wave is a way to represent invisible vibration.
library-hearing-more-1: Sound waves travel through the ear canal and vibrate the eardrum.
library-hearing-more-2: Small bones pass the vibrations on to a fluid-filled part of the inner ear.
library-hearing-more-3: Sensory cells there help make electrical signals.
library-hearing-more-4: A nerve carries them to the brain.
library-hearing-more-5: People hear in different ways and may use hearing devices, signs or other communication supports.
library-hearing-tell-1: Sound can make parts of an ear move.
library-hearing-tell-2: Tiny cells turn that motion into signals.

library-heart-deep-3: Blood returning from the body begins the circuit again.
library-heart-deep-4: Small vessels let materials move between blood and tissues.
library-heart-deep-5: Valves reduce backward flow, while an electrical signaling system coordinates the muscle’s contractions.
library-heart-deep-6: The rate changes with activity and other needs, so there is no single speed that every child must match.
library-heart-deep-7: Our two-color arrows separate the routes for learning; blood is not blue inside a person.
library-heart-deep-8: This is a model of circulation, not an instruction to measure or judge a heartbeat.
library-heart-more-1: The heart is made largely of muscle.
library-heart-more-2: It squeezes and relaxes to move blood.
library-heart-more-3: Blood travels to the lungs to exchange gases, then to the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients.
library-heart-more-4: Valves help it move in the right direction.
library-heart-more-5: The familiar heart symbol is a drawing; the real organ has a different shape.

library-heart-tell-3: Blood carries things your cells need.

library-insect-flight-deep-1: Insects are the only invertebrates with true powered flight.
library-insect-flight-deep-2: A butterfly's broad wings and a dragonfly's narrower wings work in different ways.
library-insect-flight-deep-3: Flying animals are not all close relatives.
library-insect-flight-deep-4: Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.
library-insect-flight-deep-5: Insects are the only members of this broad group with true powered flight, rather than simply drifting or gliding.
library-insect-flight-deep-6: Most insects have two pairs of wings, though some have only one pair or none.
library-insect-flight-deep-7: Veins help support the thin wing surface, and some wings have scales or other special coverings.
library-insect-flight-deep-8: Wing shape, texture, and the pattern of veins help scientists compare insects.
library-insect-flight-deep-9: Flight is a shared ability across very different animals, so it cannot by itself prove that a bat, bird, and insect are close relatives.

library-insect-flight-more-2: Moving wings push on the air and help support the insect.
library-insect-flight-more-3: Wings come in many shapes and beat at different speeds.
library-insect-flight-more-4: A bee, butterfly, and dragonfly can all fly, but their wings do not look or move exactly alike.

library-islands-deep-1: Many ocean islands are the tops of much larger landforms rising from the seafloor.
library-islands-deep-2: An island's shore can change as waves, currents, and storms move sand and other material.
library-islands-deep-3: Different islands record different geological histories.
library-islands-deep-4: Lava can build rock upward, coral growth can add limestone in shallow seas, and uplift can raise former seafloor above water.
library-islands-deep-5: Changes in sea level also change which land is exposed.
library-islands-deep-6: Building land and reshaping its edge are separate processes.
library-islands-deep-7: Waves and currents may move sand around an existing island without making the island's original bedrock.
library-islands-deep-8: A cross-section is a side view cut through a model, useful for seeing the hidden base.
library-islands-deep-9: It simplifies the many layers and changes that a real island may preserve.

library-jellyfish-move-deep-4: Jellyfish tentacles have specialized stinging cells used in feeding and defense.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-5: A stranded jellyfish or a loose tentacle can still pose a stinging risk.

library-jellyfish-move-more-2: By contracting its bell and then relaxing, it moves water and can swim.
library-jellyfish-move-more-3: Even swimming jellyfish drift with ocean currents.
library-jellyfish-move-more-4: The trailing tentacles help many kinds catch food; they are not legs for walking.

library-lever-deep-2: For a balanced simple lever, a smaller force farther from the pivot can balance a larger force closer to it.
library-lever-deep-3: When the lever moves, the end traveling farther trades that distance for force at the load.
library-lever-deep-4: Not every lever makes the needed input force smaller: other layouts help with speed or reach.
library-lever-deep-5: Real levers bend a little and have friction, so a perfect diagram leaves some effects out.
library-lever-deep-6: Our bar and triangle are a model, not instructions for lifting furniture or putting fingers near a pinch point.

library-lever-more-3: Where you push, where the load sits and where the fulcrum sits all matter.
library-lever-more-4: In some arrangements, pushing farther from the fulcrum lets a smaller force lift a load through a shorter distance.
library-lever-more-5: The lever does not create energy.

library-lightning-deep-1: Lightning can happen inside a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground.
library-lightning-deep-2: If you hear thunder, tell a grown-up and go inside a substantial building.
library-lightning-deep-4: An electrical discharge is a movement of electric charge that releases stored electrical energy.
library-lightning-deep-5: In lightning, the rapid heating makes nearby air expand and sends out a pressure wave: thunder.
library-lightning-deep-6: The flash and sound come from the same event but travel at different speeds.
library-lightning-deep-7: Lightning need not strike the ground to produce thunder; it can occur within a cloud or between clouds.
library-lightning-deep-8: A substantial building is safer than an open shelter, and being indoors still means staying away from windows and following grown-up safety directions.
library-lightning-deep-9: This explanation is not a storm-warning service or an outdoor experiment.

library-lightning-more-2: It heats the air very quickly, and the expanding air makes a sound wave called thunder.
library-lightning-more-3: We see the flash before we hear the sound because light travels faster.
library-lightning-more-4: Light gets to us faster than sound, so a distant flash is seen before its thunder is heard.

library-limestone-deep-1: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate.
library-limestone-deep-2: Some forms contain recognizable fossils, while others are made of very fine grains.
library-limestone-deep-3: Guam’s named limestone formations differ in age, texture and how they formed.
library-limestone-deep-4: Rainwater moving through cracks and pores can slowly dissolve limestone and enlarge openings.
library-limestone-deep-5: This helps explain why an aquifer can hold water within rock rather than in one giant underground tank.
library-limestone-deep-6: A small drawing of shells becoming rock skips burial, cementation and long spans of time.
library-limestone-deep-7: It also cannot identify a real rock by color alone.
library-limestone-deep-8: Leave rocks in place and avoid caves and unstable edges.
library-limestone-forest-deep-1: A limestone forest is named for the ground beneath it, not for trees made of stone.
library-limestone-forest-deep-2: Rock, soil, rainfall and living things interact.
library-limestone-forest-deep-3: Plants provide food and shelter, and new seedlings help a forest renew itself.
library-limestone-forest-deep-4: On Guam, introduced animals and invasive plants can disrupt those connections.
library-limestone-forest-deep-5: Restoration work includes choosing suitable native plants and managing threats, rather than simply planting any fast-growing tree.
library-limestone-forest-deep-6: A recovering forest may need ongoing care.
library-limestone-forest-deep-7: This illustration combines plant shapes to show layers; it is not a list of species that must grow together.
library-limestone-forest-deep-8: Follow established paths with a grown-up and leave plants where they are.
library-limestone-forest-more-1: Parts of Guam support forest on limestone ground.
library-limestone-forest-more-2: Trees, vines and other plants make a layered home for animals.
library-limestone-forest-more-3: Thin soil and openings in the rock affect where roots can grow and how water moves.
library-limestone-forest-more-4: A forest is more than a group of tall trees: smaller plants, seedlings and soil life matter too.
library-limestone-forest-tell-1: A forest can grow on limestone.
library-limestone-forest-tell-2: Roots reach into soil and cracks.
library-limestone-forest-tell-3: Leaves make shade for life below.
library-limestone-more-1: Corals, shells and other sea life can leave hard calcium carbonate parts behind.
library-limestone-more-2: Over time, such material can become limestone.
library-limestone-more-3: Much of northern Guam has limestone, including rock formed in old reef and lagoon settings.
library-limestone-more-4: Water can move through openings in it.
library-limestone-more-5: Not every limestone has visible shells, and limestone can form in other ways too.

library-limestone-tell-2: Many kinds hold bits from sea life.

library-mangrove-roots-deep-1: A mangrove forest joins land and sea rather than fitting neatly into only one.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-2: Its roots help stabilize sediments and reduce erosion in some coastal settings.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-3: Leaves and other organic material become part of a food web, while many animals use the sheltered space.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-4: Some mangroves have prop roots; others have roots that project above the mud and help gas exchange.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-5: Not every root is a drinking straw and not every mangrove removes salt the same way.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-6: Healthy mangroves can soften wave effects, but they cannot promise safety from every storm.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-7: Look from an established path with a grown-up.
library-mangrove-roots-more-1: Mangroves grow along sheltered tropical and subtropical coasts.
library-mangrove-roots-more-2: They have ways to cope with salty water and wet, low-oxygen mud.
library-mangrove-roots-more-3: Roots can slow water and trap sediment.
library-mangrove-roots-more-4: Among the roots, young fish and other animals may find shelter.

library-muscles-deep-4: The nervous system coordinates which fibers work and when.

library-native-trees-deep-2: It describes a species’ history in a region, rather than a person’s identity.
library-native-trees-deep-3: Forest recovery depends on relationships among seedlings, mature plants, animals, soil and water.
library-native-trees-deep-4: Invasive vines can crowd other plants, and introduced animals can change which seedlings survive.
library-native-trees-deep-5: Restoration teams choose plants for the habitat and manage those pressures.
library-native-trees-deep-6: Removing threats and supporting natural regrowth can matter alongside planting.

library-night-sky-day-review-1: Our marked place faces the Sun. Sunlight scattered by the air makes a bright daytime sky, so most other stars are hard to see. They are still there.
library-night-sky-limits: An invented sky, with symbolic stars, brightness and distances. Imagined lines join dots. Earth’s rotation changes a night’s view; its orbit changes seasonal views. This is not tonight’s Guam sky or a navigation chart.
library-night-sky-limits-review-1: Make a pattern of your own. These dots are invented, so the picture cannot tell you which stars are over Guam tonight.
library-night-sky-night-review-1: Keep turning Earth and watch the stars appear to shift. Our place is turning with the ground beneath it. Stop at any step to compare the view.
library-night-sky-pattern-review-1: Choose a few star dots and join them into a shape. The lines belong to your picture. Real stars that appear near one another in the sky can be far apart in space.
library-night-sky-season-review-1: Move Earth to another part of its path around the Sun. The night side now faces a different part of space. The stars people can see also depend on their place on Earth and the time of night.
library-night-sky-turn-review-1: Turn Earth until our place faces away from the Sun. The view grows dark because Earth turns, rather than the Sun going around Earth each day.
library-night-view-deep-1: Three kinds of change can affect a night view.

library-night-view-deep-3: Clouds, nearby lights and the Moon’s brightness also affect what you can notice.
library-night-view-deep-4: A model that advances one step is choosing a view for learning, not speeding up the real sky or predicting tonight’s clouds.
library-night-view-deep-5: Stars have their own motions, but the familiar sweep during one night mainly comes from our turning viewpoint.

library-night-view-more-3: During a night, Earth’s turn makes stars appear to move across our view.
library-night-view-more-4: Across the year, Earth’s trip around the Sun changes which direction the night side faces, so different stars can be visible.

library-salty-deep-2: Ocean water contains many dissolved salts, not just the salt we sprinkle on food.
library-salty-deep-3: Different places can have different saltiness.
library-salty-deep-4: Rainwater is slightly acidic, which helps it break down rocks and release dissolved particles called ions.
library-salty-deep-5: Rivers carry these ions toward the ocean.
library-salty-deep-6: Reactions between seawater and hot rocks at seafloor openings add some materials and remove others.
library-salty-deep-7: Salinity is a measure of the salts dissolved in water.
library-salty-deep-8: Evaporation removes water rather than most of those salts, while incoming fresh water can dilute seawater.
library-salty-deep-9: Saltiness therefore reflects several processes happening together, not just one river adding ordinary table salt to a motionless sea.

library-saturn-deep-2: Its rings look bright because they reflect sunlight.
library-saturn-deep-3: Other giant planets have rings too, though Saturn's are especially easy to notice in pictures.
library-saturn-deep-4: Gravity holds the ring particles in orbit, just as it helps hold moons around planets.
library-saturn-deep-5: Reflected sunlight makes the icy pieces visible; the rings do not shine like a star.
library-saturn-deep-6: Saturn has no solid surface like Earth's ground, so a picture of a neat ball is a simplified view of a gas giant.
library-saturn-deep-7: The ring system includes gaps and bands rather than a single uniform strip.

library-seagrass-deep-2: Like plants on land, seagrasses need suitable growing conditions.
library-seagrass-deep-3: Boats and trampling can damage a meadow.
library-seagrass-deep-4: Seagrasses have roots, leaves, and flowers, even though they spend their lives underwater.
library-seagrass-deep-5: A buried horizontal stem called a rhizome can grow along the seabed and send up new shoots.
library-seagrass-deep-6: This lets a meadow spread as connected plant growth as well as through seeds.
library-seagrass-deep-7: The leaves make food using sunlight through photosynthesis.

library-seasons-deep-10: The familiar four-season description also does not describe every place's weather equally well, especially in tropical regions.

library-seasons-deep-3: Near the tropics, wet and dry patterns may be more noticeable than snowy winters.
library-seasons-deep-4: Earth's axis keeps a similar direction in space during its yearly orbit.
library-seasons-deep-5: When one hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, its sunlight is more direct and its days are generally longer.
library-seasons-deep-6: The other hemisphere has the opposite pattern.

library-water-journey-cool-review-1: As moist air cools enough, some water vapor turns into tiny liquid drops. This is condensation. Many drops together make a visible cloud; clouds can also contain ice.
library-water-journey-flow-review-1: Water underground can move through connected pores and cracks. Some reaches the ocean; some stays stored much longer than our quick picture shows.
library-water-journey-freeze-review-1: Cool liquid water enough and it can freeze into ice. Salt makes seawater freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water. Our model skips the wait and temperature measurements.
library-water-journey-grow-review-1: Tiny cloud drops can join and grow. Once they fall fast enough to leave the cloud, they become rain. Ice crystals can grow and fall too.
library-water-journey-heat-review-1: Some water at the surface becomes an invisible gas called water vapor. Energy from the Sun helps this change, called evaporation. The water left behind can stay in the sea.
library-water-journey-limits: A simplified set of possible water paths. Sizes and travel times are symbolic, and plants and many other routes are left out. Water vapor is invisible; cloud drops or ice are visible. This is not a forecast or a drinking-water guide.
library-water-journey-limits-review-1: Choose a new route. Water can move through plants, air, ground and sea, with many different stops along the way. A real journey has no set starting point or travel time.
library-water-journey-melt-review-1: Add enough heat and ice melts into liquid water. Freezing and melting change how the water molecules are arranged; they are still water.
library-water-journey-runoff-review-1: Water that flows over the ground is called runoff. Follow it downhill toward a stream or the sea. The shape and surface of the land help set its path.
library-water-journey-soak-review-1: Rain can soak into soil and cracks in rock. Some stays near plant roots. Some travels deeper, through spaces that let water pass.
library-water-journey-warm-review-1: Cloud droplets can evaporate back into invisible water vapor. Try this path: a cloud can shrink away before it makes rain.
